description: We are OrbitaFire, a team of 3 students from UTEC (Lima, Peru) with skills in statistics, time series, machine learning, databases and web development. We are harmonizing 20+ years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots from MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent series, shown as an interactive burning calendar with anomaly alerts and 1-3 month forecasts. Pilot: the Peruvian Amazon and Andes. We welcome people with skills in web development, design or video storytelling.
summary: OrbitaFire joins 25 years of NASA fire data into one comparable record for Peru and warns when a Communal Reserve burns more than usual. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) count fire differently: VIIRS detects 4 to 8 times more hotspots, so old and new numbers cannot be compared. We trained a Poisson model on 2012–2026, when both satellites fly, to express every MODIS month as a VIIRS-equivalent value with a 95% uncertainty band. Validated year by year, its worst yearly error is 17.7%, against 31.1% for a constant factor. The harmonized record shows 2024 was Peru's record fire year (95,270 hotspots, 1.5 times a typical year) and that the surroundings of the Amarakaeri Communal Reserve had 2.8 times their normal fire. A free bilingual website turns this into maps, a 3D time explorer and alerts for the park rangers of SERNANP and the Indigenous communities who co-manage Peru's Communal Reserves.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

OrbitaFire joins 25 years of NASA fire data into one comparable record for Peru (2000–2026) and shows, on a free bilingual website, where and when fire activity is higher than usual — with a focus on the Amazon and Peru's Communal Reserves.

HOW IT WORKS

MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) detect fire differently: VIIRS sees 4 to 8 times more hotspots, so old and new counts cannot be compared directly. We aggregated NASA FIRMS hotspots (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m from S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) on a 0.25° grid by month and trained a Poisson regression on 2012–2026, when both sensors fly, to express every MODIS month as a VIIRS-equivalent value with a 95% uncertainty band. A separate Terra-only model covers 2000–2002. Leave-one-year-out validation gives a worst yearly error of 17.7% (vs 31.1% for a constant conversion factor), a mean error of 8.5% and a Spearman correlation of 0.89. Each cell and month is then compared with its own typical season using a robust z-score, producing clear categories (normal, unusual, exceptional).

KEY FINDINGS

- 2024 was Peru's record fire year: 95,270 hotspots, 1.5 times a typical year; September 2024 alone had 36,394.

- 81% of grid cells were above their typical season in 2024.

- Around the Amarakaeri Communal Reserve, 2024 had 196 hotspots, 2.8 times its normal level.

- In October 2026, the buffer zone of the Ashaninka Communal Reserve had 220 hotspots vs 51 typical (exceptional).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Park rangers of SERNANP and the Indigenous communities who co-manage Communal Reserves can see in seconds whether their territory is burning more than usual, compare any month with 25 years of history, and prioritize patrols and prevention. Everything is open, free, works on mobile and needs no login.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, statsmodels, GeoPandas) for processing and modeling; JavaScript, Leaflet and MapLibre GL for the 2D map and 3D time explorer; NASA GIBS and EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless basemaps; GitHub Pages for free static hosting.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

Instead of another raw hotspot map, we answer a simple question: "Is this normal for here and now?" We report uncertainty honestly, use plain-language labels in English and Spanish, and use only official public boundaries from SERNANP. We do not portray Indigenous communities as causes of fire: they appear as partners in protecting their territory.

Live site: https://jeanluka17.github.io/orbitafire/

Code and data: https://github.com/JeanLuka17/orbitafire
